condition.label: cervical radicular pain
condition.distinctions: Cervical nerve-root-related arm/neck pain is distinct from nonspecific neck pain, cord disease, WAD and postoperative rehabilitation.

scope.population: Cervical radiculopathy onset under one month; Confirmed cervical radiculopathy
scope.stage: Varies by source; acute/recent versus chronic and symptom irritability are explicitly retained. Unknown stage remains unknown.
scope.operativeStatus: Nonsurgical evidence predominates; no postoperative protocol approved or inferred.
scope.exclusions: Source-specific exclusions are applicability boundaries, not diagnosis-wide contraindications. Coexisting conditions and independently selected joint limits retain precedence.
scope.uncertainty:
- Ordinary training: when nerve-root irritability is active, alter demand/position according to assessed symptom response and capacity; this is clinical-guidance inference (CR-G1), not proof overhead lifting or all cervical extension is intrinsically harmful. No numeric cervical ROM/load ceiling established.
- Supportive candidates: clinician-guided low-load neck control/endurance; general physical activity can be a candidate, not automatically contraindicated. Neurodynamic tensioning/sliding are clinically distinct and cannot be generated from generic stretches.
- Restriction-only/research draft until diagnosis, neurological status, stage and clinically reviewed thresholds are known. Progressive deficit or possible myelopathy requires assessment, not automated progression. Specific urgent criteria need a separately approved clinical pathway rather than being reverse-engineered from trial exclusions.
- No evidence retrieved to authorize postoperative exercise; prior surgery is an attribute requiring its own orders. NASS 2010 is older; 2024 Dutch and 2025 synthesis used for currentness.

sources.design: Final Dutch NVvN guideline exercise module, published 24 July 2024
sources.population: Cervical radicular syndrome; assessment and stage-specific care
sources.comparator: Exercise versus wait-and-see/other exercise in underpinning studies
sources.outcomes: Dutch NVvN cervical radicular syndrome guideline, final July 24, 2024. Exercise module. FT module. Consider targeted exercise with a suitably experienced therapist; low-certainty pain/disability evidence, very-low/absent evidence for several outcomes/harms. Initial reactive phase prioritizes advice to avoid aggravation; subacute active approach respects individual capacity; later self-management. This clinical stage advice does not yield a fixed extension/rotation or lifting ban. Evidence synthesis finds little/no additional disability benefit over wait-and-see or other exercise. Unknown stage should not become an invented “approved” neck-strengthening routine.

sources.harms: Low/very-low or absent evidence for several outcomes including harms
sources.limitations: Stage and capacity advice is clinical guidance, not fixed extension/rotation/load limits Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

protocol.progression: Reactive stage avoids aggravation; subacute active approach within capacity; later self-management

sources.population: Cervical radiculopathy onset under one month
sources.comparator: Collar/rest versus physiotherapy/home exercise versus wait-and-see
sources.coInterventions: Rest/collar or therapist-led graded care according to arm
sources.outcomes: Kuijper et al., 2009 RCT. DOI 10.1136/bmj.b3883, BMJ full article. Substantive full article text available in search result; direct open subsequently 403. 205 recent-onset (<1 month) cervical radiculopathy patients; collar/rest, PT/home exercises, or wait-and-see; six-week treatment, six-month follow-up. Hands-off graded mobilizing/stabilizing/strengthening PT twice weekly. Arm/neck pain reduction over six weeks favored collar or PT (~12–17 mm/100 difference); little/no persistent between-group difference by six months. Adverse-event outcome absent per CR-G1's synthesis. Collar/rest arm's short-term efficacy does not justify app-imposed immobilization, especially when applying a different neck-pain diagnosis or recovery stage.
sources.uncertainty: Direct BMJ fetch 403 after indexed substantive article text; conservative abstract-only serialization; short-term pain benefit did not establish persistent superiority
sources.harms: Adverse-event outcome absent per CR-G1 synthesis
sources.limitations: Direct BMJ fetch 403 after indexed substantive article text; conservative abstract-only serialization; short-term pain benefit did not establish persistent superiority Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

sources.comparator: Neck-specific training versus prescribed general physical activity
sources.outcomes: Dedering et al., 2018 RCT. DOI 10.1016/j.apmr.2018.06.008, PMID 30473018. Abstract; protocol details additionally inspected in CR-G1 and CR-S1, not primary FT. 144 confirmed CR patients; three-month neck-specific training versus prescribed general physical activity; both behavioral approach, outcomes 3/6/12/24 months. No significant group or group×time effects; both improved. Guideline describes progression from gentle isometrics to low-load endurance, response-tailored, three sessions/week; comparator aerobic/muscular activity ~30 min three times/week. Primary detailed harms unavailable. Supports several possible active pathways, not superiority of one specific execution or a blanket general-activity ban.

sources.outcomes: Mallard et al., 2022 updated OPTIMa review. DOI 10.2340/jrm.v54.2799, PMID 35797062, FT PMC9422871. FT relevant synthesis. Four acceptable RCTs and one low-quality RCT, adults recent/any-duration radiculopathy; multimodal rehabilitation compared with traction, general activity, injection or surgery-containing care. Review's short-term pairwise signal favoring multimodal rehabilitation is compatible with the original trial's nonsignificant overall group/time model; do not present as decisive superiority.
